draft.title: Compound interest with regular additions
card: This investment earns compound interest, and the same amount is also added at the end of every period. The balance grows from both.
Each period: new balance = old balance × (1 + r) + deposit, where r is the interest rate for one period as a decimal. Divide an annual rate by the number of periods in a year.
Example: start with $1000, interest 10% per year, add $200 at the end of each year. After year 1: 1000 × 1.10 + 200 = $1300.
After year 2: 1300 × 1.10 + 200 = $1630. The interest is worked out on the whole balance, including earlier deposits and earlier interest.
draft.remember: Multiply the balance by (1 + r), then add the deposit, and repeat.

a.q: An account has $2000, earns 5% per year, and $500 is added at the end of each year. What is the balance after year 1?
a.why: New balance = 2000 × 1.05 + 500 = 2100 + 500 = $2600. $2500 is wrong because it adds the deposit but skips the interest. $2100 is the balance with interest only, with the deposit left out.
a.clue: Add the interest first, then the deposit.

b.q: Priya opens a savings account with $1000. It earns 6% per year, and she adds $100 at the end of each year. What is the balance after year 2?
b.why: Year 1: 1000 × 1.06 + 100 = $1160. Year 2: 1160 × 1.06 + 100 = 1229.60 + 100 = $1329.60 is the balance, so check: 1160 × 1.06 = 1229.60, giving $1329.60. None of the options match, so this question needs to be redone.
b.clue: Work out year 1 first, then use that balance for year 2.
